chapter: Original Dixieland Jazz Band in New York
title: Signorelli, Memphis Five, and Reisenweber's Broadway years
summary: La Rocca recalls the Margie plug dispute, hiring Frank Signorelli, how the Memphis Five copied the band's arrangements, and the 1917 Reisenweber's engagement, money and clientele.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Well, we forgot about Lytel and Frankie Signorelli. About 1920, Signorelli joined my band. At that time they may have had a Memphis Five, but I never heard of them stopping the machine. Well, I had a little bit of friction with Roberson. He had promised the band a thousand dollars if I put Margie over. Well, I saw the plug of Margie for him, sang it for him, placed it on the record for him, and after he got his first statement, he didn't say anything. I asked him about what he was going to do to three of them. That was Conrad and Benny Davis, and he, what he gave us, a thousand dollars for plugging his tune. I was in the band business to make money. I wasn't out just to play somebody's number when I had other numbers of my own, unless I was going to get something out of them. So it was promised by the three of us we were to get this money, and I asked Roberson for the money. He didn't say nothing. He just ignored me, just kept on playing his piano. The next day I gave him his two weeks' notice, and I replaced him. This was at the Follinsbergine with Frank Signorelli, who I had tried out in a song plugger's place, or in other words, a publisher's place. In that time they had little rooms where you could go in and listen to music. Well this boy knew all our numbers from the recordings, and he was a very good pianist, and he had got the rhythm down pretty good. And we hired him. Frankie stood with me from 1920, part of 1920, 21, and 22. We went to Balconnates, and after about six or eight weeks there I became ill with the flute. And I pulled the band out. It was here that the Memphis Five got their foothold on Broadway through the efforts of Frank Signorelli, and Jimmy Lytel, who had replaced Shields after Shields thought he had enough money and left the band. And I don't know where he went, whether he went to Chicago, California, I don't know. I have never corresponded with him at any time since then. It was here that the Memphis Five got the job at the Balconnates. But prior to that they had made recordings for Sam Lanham, and the lads, seven black aces or something on that order. And they had copied every arrangement. Through Frank Signorelli, he knew the arrangements, how we played them, and from this clarinet player. It was easy for Philly Napoleon and the rest of them, like Nick Moore, to fall in line on these arrangements, because the piano player had learned them. And that was the beginning of the Memphis Five big history in the world. I remember when Philly Napoleon came to me around 1918, he used to beg me to show him how to make slurs in different passages on the clarinet. That's before I knew they had a Memphis Five. And I used to help him out. I helped a fellow named Frank Garanti. I helped Big Spider-Vac. In fact, I started him on the trumpet, Big Spider-Vac. I was a kid. Many people said it's not so. But this boy came to New York when he was 17 years of age. And he wouldn't let him in, Rising Webbers. He was too young. And he told the doorkeeper, because Rising Webbers at this time was a 400 club. You couldn't get in there unless you had a pass. And there was a dollar cover charge. It's the only place that had a dollar cover charge on Broadway. And you had to be exclusive to come into that room. And we played. We played in there since 1917, January 15 or 17 we opened there. But we was in New York before January 15 because we didn't have tuxedos to open there. We had to go get tuxedos, photographs and stuff. We were in a big time there. And in our first two weeks' tryout they tried us in the paradise. Some of the ads in the paper might spell J-A-S-Z. Some of them spell J-A-S. Some is J-A-S-S. And some is J-A-Z-Z. While it was in Webbers. And the kind of people who visited that place was all the great actors like Charlie Chaplin, all many, every big star that played on Broadway. And Franklin Simons spent money in there like water. The Gould family. It was an exclusive room at Joanna. We were given a thousand dollars a week. When we made, on our collections, in the kiddie box that we used to have called a sugar can, sometime a hundred to two hundred dollars per night. They may dispute me on this but this is the truth. Now, if these bands in New Orleans existed, with all this loot going around, giving out in New York, and men like Ted Lewis, Ross Garner, Lopez, Vincent Lopez, former jazz bands, who copied after the style of the original Dixieland jazz bands recording, replacing these Negroes that had full sway because when we arrived there, Broadway was black. They had no white bands hardly at all playing on Broadway. They were all Negroes playing what they call syncopated or ragtime music. Now they say this music didn't exist anywhere else but New York, but it did. Because the way I copied from the records from Susan, others copied the same. There was no difference. Because I had read that article that someone sent me, that Louis Armstrong had an arm full of records and he was listening to them, and he copied from them. And nobody can tell me these other niggas didn't copy from them. If there's so many white men copied from the recordings of this band, which I'm going to try to play if we have enough time today, how these idioms got into this music. Going back to the Memphis Five, we used to play a tune called, Shemmy Like My Sister Kate, that A.J. P. Ronge sent to me. If my talk ain't chronological, I can't help it because my mind don't work like an educated man. I'm only telling you from heart. I have no script in front of you. I'll ask you, do I read from a script?
